title: Computer Vision Advances in Monitoring Multi‐Species Invertebrate Fisheries in the Pacific
content:
ABSTRACT

Monitoring diverse, dispersed small-scale invertebrate fisheries remains challenging because taxonomic diversity, informal trade and dispersed harvesting limit sustained programs that can capture standardised data used for catch identification and measurement. Computer vision is increasingly being used to overcome these challenges, but most affordable and accessible single-camera systems face a trade-off: close-range imagery required for high fidelity species identification while increasing parallax error for three-dimensional specimens. We tested a hardware-agnostic calibration method to improve an automated fisheries-monitoring platform. Nationally standardised coins placed on specimens provided a local, distance-independent scale reference. Manual, coin-corrected and uncorrected computer-vision measurements of carapace length in spiny lobsters (Panulirus penicillatus) were compared using linear mixed-effects models. Coin correction removed systematic bias, reducing mean percentage error from 10.77% to 1.20% and mean absolute error from 8.6 to 2.3 mm. By contrast, linear-regression correction for Panulirus penicillatus under-corrected small lobsters and over-corrected large individuals, biasing Length-Based Spawning Potential Ratio estimates. Where remote observers could verify species-level labels, computer-vision classification exceeded 90% accuracy, with other performance metrics scoring above 80%. Performance on unfiltered operational data depended on image acquisition: close-range board imagery substantially outperformed greater-distance mat imagery for taxa requiring fine diagnostic detail, particularly bivalves and gastropods. Coplanar calibration is therefore necessary for 2D computer-vision systems to provide reliable species identification and morphometric data simultaneously, supporting scalable, field-appropriate monitoring of multi-species invertebrate fisheries in data-limited small-island developing states.
